proof:
# Sharp unequal-weight extension of the three-fiber residual threshold
nearest-neighbor structure in the one-dimensional KKT reduction matters;
it is not a claim that every arbitrary barycentric row obeys midpoint bounds.

Let d>=1, let 0<w<1, and let A,K,B be positive-volume compact convex
bodies in R^d satisfying w A+(1-w)B subset K. Suppose none of their
three volumes exceeds half their sum. Put c=|K|^(1/d), and let one
actual halfspace have affine thresholds at the two endpoint bases and
the weighted source base. Write its source captured fraction as p and
its strict residual roots as f_A,f_K,f_B.

For 0<t<1 let kappa_d(t) be the unique solution k in (t,1) of

    (k/t)^d-((1-k)/(1-t))^d=1.                           (1)

Then with t=max(w,1-w),

    [w f_A+(1-w) f_B-f_K]_+
       <=c[kappa_d(t)-(1-p)^(1/d)]_+.                  (2)

Both the full positive-gap profile and its threshold

    eta_d(w)=1-kappa_d(max(w,1-w))^d                    (3)

are sharp. Under strict three-fiber noheavy assumptions the profile
remains the supremal bound and the threshold remains optimal.

To prove this, normalize c=1 and write a=|A|^(1/d), b=|B|^(1/d).
BM gives wa+(1-w)b<=1. If a<=1, then wa<=w<kappa_d(w). Otherwise
b<=(1-wa)/(1-w), and a^d<=1+b^d gives

    (wa/w)^d-((1-wa)/(1-w))^d<=1,

hence wa<=kappa_d(w). The same argument with the endpoints exchanged
gives (1-w)b<=kappa_d(1-w). The left side of(1) is strictly increasing
in k, equals0 at k=t, and exceeds1 at k=1, so its root exists uniquely.
For fixed k its derivative in t is

    -d k^d/t^(d+1)-d(1-k)^d/(1-t)^(d+1)<0.

Consequently kappa_d(t) is strictly increasing in t. This proves

    max(wa,(1-w)b)<=kappa_d(max(w,1-w)).                 (4)

If both endpoint strict residuals are nonempty, residual BM gives
f_K>=w f_A+(1-w)f_B, using compact strict truncations and continuity
from below. If at least one is empty, there is at most one positive
term on the left. Inequality(4) then proves(2). No empty set is inserted
into a BM inequality.

For exact sharpness take t=max(w,1-w), k=kappa_d(t), and give the
endpoint with weight t the root a=k/t>1 and the other endpoint the
root b=(1-k)/(1-t)<1. With a common volume-one convex body T, choose
those endpoint bodies to be aT and bT, and set K=T. Their weighted
Minkowski combination is exactly T, and a^d=1+b^d by(1). Thus the
larger endpoint has exactly half of the three marked fiber masses;
the other two satisfy strict noheavy inequalities. A sufficiently
large integer-coordinate tilt of one common halfspace makes that
larger endpoint entirely residual and the other entirely captured,
while retaining any prescribed own-fiber captured fraction p. This
achieves equality in(2).

For w rational, choose integer endpoint bases on either side of0
whose barycentric weights there are w,1-w, and take their actual
lifted convex hull. Its source section is exactly T. It can have
additional integer fibers; the stated noheavy hypothesis and theorem
concern the three marked fibers only. For w=1/2 the bases can be -1,1,
and those three are the entire integer base. For arbitrary real w,
the identical construction works at real endpoint bases.

To make noheavy strict, slightly decrease a while keeping a>1 and
set b=(1-ta)/(1-t). The strict inequality a^d<1+b^d then holds, the
other two noheavy inequalities remain strict, and the resulting
profile approaches(2). Thus no larger threshold can hold even under
strict noheaviness.

At w=1/2, kappa_d(1/2)=B_d/2, with
B_d^d-(2-B_d)^d=1, recovering the sharp midpoint theorem. However
kappa_d(t)->1 as t->1, so the threshold tends to zero for increasingly
uneven rows.

For a fully exact comparison take d=2 and w=3/4. Then

    kappa=(18-3sqrt(2))/16,
    a=(6-sqrt(2))/4,
    b=(3sqrt(2)-2)/4,
    eta=(54sqrt(2)-43)/128.

Here (3/4)a+(1/4)b=1, a^2-b^2=1, and
kappa>3/4>sqrt(5)/3=(1-gamma_2)^(1/2). Therefore an own-fiber canonical
simplex cap fraction gamma_2=4/9 can still violate the unequal-weight
residual comparison, even though all three marked volumes are nonheavy.
No global criticality or global deepest-center assertion is made for
this unequal-weight sharpness example. The separate critical nearest-
neighbor theorem uses those genuinely global conditions and equal weights.
